comments.value: I would love to know what the actual limits are for each rating, and ya i agree with godfall on this one.

I actually don't want this because the only way I can imagine this can go is that they make the poly limit restriction even more restricted.

32k for excellent

70k or less for good, medium, poor

70,001 for vpoor

to change this is just going to make good, medium, poor requirements more restricted.

the natural change would be something like

30k excellent

40k good

50k medium

60k poor

70k+1 vpoor

that restricts creators more

if you go the other way, then we'd have

32k excellent

70k good

100k medium

130k poor

160k+ vpoor

now all avatars across the board are theoretically unoptimized or a little heavier no matter how many tri you add

The Core Problem

Right now in VRChat:

70,000 tris or less = "Good" rating

70,001+ = instantly "Very Poor"

This binary jump discourages optimization and leads to frustration. Why bother optimizing shaders, materials, and dynamic bones if one triangle tips the scale?

Godfall's Proposal (More Lenient)

Good: ≤ 70k

Medium: ~90k

Poor: ~120k

VPoor: >120k

This is flexible and creator-friendly, but Chdata is worried it could:

Encourage bloat

Lead to VRC tightening restrictions instead

Result in “Medium” and “Poor” avatars being the new average, raising system strain

Chdata's Counter-Proposal (More Restrictive)

Excellent: ≤ 30k

Good: ≤ 40k

Medium: ≤ 50k

Poor: ≤ 60k

VPoor: > 70k

This tightens limits and would likely force most custom avatars into VPoor, including those already considered well-optimized.

My In-Between Suggestion That I feel would fit better:

Excellent: ≤ 32k (same)

Good: ≤ 70k (same)

Medium: 70–80k

Poor: 80–100k

VPoor: >100k

In my opinion this is honestly the most realistic and balanced option:

Maintains existing standards up to 70k

Offers a buffer between Medium and Poor that reflects actual optimization effort

Avoids penalizing creators for going slightly over

Still discourages truly bloated avatars

Why This Makes Sense

Polygon count isn’t the only factor in performance. Avatar complexity is multifaceted (materials, bones, physics, etc.).

Hard cutoffs are demotivating. Gradual thresholds encourage creators to optimize as much as they can without being punished for going over by 1 triangle.

Balanced thresholds support VRChat’s goals of both performance and user freedom.
when are we fixing this boys, it wont take long cmon

Honestly the main thing stopping me from prioritizing optimization is that its gonna be very poor anyways.

I might eventually do it (though I do always optimize texture use) but for the most part I just rarely see the point if the rating is going to be very poor anyways.

May latest model I did optimize and everything is medium or good even in my least stripped down version of it but its very poor which just kind of demoralizes me to optimize anything unless I can make it good (which is maybe 1 out of 10 projects at most).

I think it is necessary to review the polygon count limit in mobile versions such as Quest.

In fact, even if it reaches 70,000 polygons, the uncompressed size will not increase much, and I think that in the mobile version, the performance rank should be Medium until it reaches 40,000 polygons.

In fact, if you try to limit the number of polygons to 15,000, which is within the default display limit of Medium in the mobile version, the appearance will be greatly disrupted.

Even with 20,000 polygons that fit into Poor, the appearance will collapse depending on the combination of costume and avatar.

I think this really highlights why VRChat’s performance ranking should move beyond just polygon caps and start including mesh VRAM usage in its evaluation.

Take my avatar as an example (tested with Thry’s Avatar VRAM Calculator):

Polygon count: ~257k (way above the 70k “Very Poor” cutoff)

Mesh memory size: only 36.44 MiB

Texture memory: ~109.86 MiB

Total VRAM load: ~146.3 MiB

So even though the polycount instantly throws it into “Very Poor,” the actual mesh memory usage is still in a reasonable range. In fact, 40 copies of this avatar in a world would take ~5.7 GiB of VRAM — which is heavy, but not catastrophic for most modern GPUs.

Compare that to a 70k poly avatar with a crap ton of blendshapes: the VRAM usage could easily surpass mine because every blendshape multiplies the vertex data stored in memory. That’s why VRAM load is a more accurate measure of performance impact than raw triangles.

A smarter performance ranking system could look like this:

Excellent: < 30 MB mesh memory

Good: < 70 MB

Medium: < 100 MB

Poor: < 130 MB

Very Poor: > 130 MB

That way, optimized high-poly avatars (with low blendshape overhead) wouldn’t be unfairly punished, while low-poly but blendshape-heavy avatars would be ranked more realistically.

Bottom line: Counting polys alone is too blunt of a tool — VRAM mesh size gives a fairer, more performance-accurate metric.
@{628f382758d3b40b66ffaa22|full_name} I agree with these values. Much more reasonable. Or VRChat could have an actually useful performance ranking system with draw calls considered.

I generally agree with this opinion.

I'll leave the middle number up to the developers, but I think the Very Poor line could be raised to around 100,000.

I also think now is the time to reinstate the polygon upload limit so that users don't take that limit for granted.

However, I think the number should be increased to 500,000, or even a more lenient 1 million.

Just like the TextMemory limit is 500MB.

(Personally, I think a limit of around 300,000 would be fine, but I think there are many players who don't agree, so we need to be careful.)

In many cases, people who can't even manage the most understandable number, the number of polygons, often end up with equally poor textures and PhysBones.

Rather than limiting the polygons themselves, we should reinstate the limit, saying, "If you can't even manage easy-to-understand numbers, you don't deserve to upload."

I would prefer that polygon limits and other settings would be accumulated into an overall score, and you would be able to see how 'performant' your avatar is by taking a well weighted average score of each component. certain things like polygons would have a larger impact and ideally scale non-linearly, with materials being similar. though other things such as particles and GPU instanced objects maybe not. it is bizarre that a single light places you within the same performance bracket as someone with Poor in each individual category.

I would support that “Medium” gets freedom up to at least 90K and “poor” at least up to 120K.

I speak from knowledge of optimizing own Avatars for (PC & Mobile), where I use only 3 Materials for PC (one with all the default atlas-texture, one for all the transparent atlas-textures and one for all the glowing atlas-textures), for the Avatar, Items and Clothing-pieces you want to hold or wear.

Furthermore, I weight-painted them to the Avatar and scaled them down to “0.013”, making them to a shape key, so I can scale them in Unity later up as a toggle animation. This lowers already the amount of Skinned Mesh Renderers, Mesh Renderers and Material Slots, but it sadly won’t solve the 70K limit you reach by just adding another cool hat to your avatar.

details:
Currently, you can have an avatar rated as “Good” at 70,000 polygons, but adding even a single triangle beyond that will instantly drop the rating to “Very Poor.”

Obviously, this doesn’t make much sense and can actually discourage some people from optimizing their avatars. (Why bother optimizing other stats if the polycount alone tanks the rating the moment you go over?)

I’d like to suggest increasing the polygon thresholds for Medium and Poor ratings, with a gradual step-up between each level. This would make a lot more sense and give creators more flexibility!

I’d really love to see this system improved.

The VRC team should ultimately decide on the final values through proper testing, but personally, I think a Poor rating could go up to around 120k, and Medium could sit around 90k.

Of course, those numbers are just based on my experience, and I’m sure the team can come up with even better thresholds through data and testing.
title: Incremental Triangle Limit for Performance Rankings
